chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
title: Leroy Smith's society band
summary: Leroy Smith's Detroit-born violinist-led band played society jobs, its members were aloof gentlemen, and Wilbur De Paris played trombone.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: Oh, definitely. And we had a black band in New York that played those jobs, too, way back.
What was the name of that band?
Leroy Smith.
Leroy Smith, a society band.
'Moonlight Cocktail'; not Twilight Time.
That's right. We called him the white Guy Lombardo, in a way.
A black Guy Lombardo.
I mean the black Guy Lombardo. I didn't mean the white. Oh, my goodness, what am I saying? (Laughter.) But he was the black Guy Lombardo.
Describe Leroy Smith.
Leroy Smith was a little guy, kind of hunchbacked, and he played violin.
Right.
A perfect gentleman. He was from Detroit.
He wasn't a hunchback but he was bowed over?
Well, yeah. Uh-huh, like that, yeah. And he held his head, you know, --
Yeah.
-- like that.
He had a curve in his back.
Yes, uh-huh. He had a very, very good band and the saxophone players all doubled. They doubled on all the instruments.
They were out of Buffalo somewhere?
Well, they started out in Detroit. He
came from Detroit, but he got his band in New York.
I see.
Yeah.
Now, Wilbur de Paris was the trombone player with that band. You know I spoke of him a good while back.
Yes, yes.
He was the trombone player with that band. But I never got to meet any of the other guys because they never came around.
Yeah, they --

They weren't guys that hung out, you know. They were above hanging out, you know. You know, they were so society conscious themselves, you know. Very clean-cut guys, perfect gentlemen, every one of them, and if you saw them, they was impeccably neat.
Cool dudes.
Oh, yes, oh, yes. That's what we would call them now.
Yes.
